questions.stem: What two parts make up the passé composé?
options: A subject pronoun and an infinitive
An auxiliary verb and a past participle
questions.explanation: The passé composé is built from « avoir » or « être » in the present, plus a past participle: « j'ai mangé », « je suis allé ». It is a compound tense, which is exactly what its name says.

questions.stem: Which auxiliary do most verbs use in the passé composé?
questions.explanation: The large majority take « avoir ». A limited set takes « être » — mostly verbs of movement and change of state, plus all reflexives — and that set is short enough to memorise.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of « manger »?
questions.explanation: Regular -er verbs form the participle by replacing -er with -é. « Mangeais » is imperfect, « mangera » future and « mangeant » the present participle — four different forms from one stem.

questions.stem: Which tense does « je mangeais » use?
questions.explanation: The -ais ending marks the imperfect, used for what used to happen or was ongoing. The passé composé would be « j'ai mangé », a compound form with an auxiliary.

questions.stem: What does the ending -rai signal, as in « je mangerai »?
questions.explanation: The simple future is the infinitive plus -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont. The conditional uses the same stem with imperfect endings, so « je mangerais » with -ais is 'I would eat' — one letter apart in writing.

questions.stem: Which auxiliary does « aller » take in the passé composé?
questions.explanation: « Aller » is one of the movement verbs taking « être »: « je suis allé ». The DR MRS VANDERTRAMP mnemonic collects the whole group, and reflexive verbs take « être » too.

questions.stem: In « elle est allée », why does the participle end in -ée?
options: It agrees with the direct object
It marks the sentence as plural
It agrees with the feminine subject because the auxiliary is « être »
questions.explanation: With « être », the participle agrees with the subject in gender and number. With « avoir » it normally does not — « elle a mangé » stays unchanged. Which auxiliary you used decides whether agreement applies.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'we went to Paris'?
questions.explanation: « Aller » takes « être », and the participle then agrees with « nous », adding -s. Two wrong options use « avoir »; the third uses the right auxiliary but forgets the agreement.

questions.stem: Which tense suits 'I used to play football every Saturday'?
questions.explanation: Repeated or habitual action in the past is imperfect territory. The passé composé would describe one completed event — 'I played football on Saturday' — and the difference in English is 'used to'.

questions.stem: Which tense suits 'I broke my arm last year'?
questions.explanation: A single completed event with a clear endpoint takes the passé composé. The imperfect would suggest it was ongoing or repeated, which for a broken arm would be an odd thing to say.

questions.stem: What does « je voudrais » mean, and which tense is it?
questions.explanation: The conditional softens a request, which is why « je voudrais » is the polite form in a shop or café and « je veux » sounds abrupt. Tense choice here is a matter of manners as much as grammar.

questions.stem: In « je le vois », what does « le » refer to?
questions.explanation: Direct object pronouns are le, la, les; indirect are lui and leur. French places them before the verb, where English puts them after — 'I see him' becomes literally 'I him see'.

questions.stem: Where does a direct object pronoun go in a French sentence?
options: At the start of the sentence
At the end of the sentence
questions.explanation: « Je le vois », not 'je vois le'. This is one of the clearest places French word order departs from English, and putting the pronoun after the verb is the most persistent English-speaker error.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I get up at seven'?
options: Je me lever à sept heures
Me je lève à sept heures
Je me lève à sept heures
questions.explanation: « Se lever » is reflexive, so the pronoun « me » must appear and sits before the verb. Dropping it changes the meaning to raising something else, and English gives you no reason to expect it.

questions.stem: Which auxiliary do reflexive verbs take in the passé composé?
questions.explanation: All reflexives take « être »: « je me suis levé ». That means the participle usually agrees with the subject too, so a female speaker writes « je me suis levée ».

questions.stem: What does « depuis » mean in « J'habite ici depuis trois ans »?
options: During — and the verb becomes imperfect
For / since — and the verb stays in the present
Ago — and the verb goes into the past
Until — and the verb goes into the future
questions.explanation: French uses the present with « depuis » for something still going on: literally 'I live here since three years'. English switches to 'have lived', so translating tense for tense produces the wrong form.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'she has eaten the apple'?
questions.explanation: « Manger » takes « avoir », and with « avoir » the participle does not agree with a following direct object. Adding the -e is the classic over-correction from someone who has just learned agreement.

questions.stem: Which sentence means 'if I had money, I would travel'?
options: Si j'avais de l'argent, je voyagerai
Si j'avais de l'argent, je voyagerais
Si j'ai de l'argent, je voyagerais
Si j'aurais de l'argent, je voyagerais
questions.explanation: The pattern is fixed: « si » plus imperfect, then conditional. Putting a conditional after « si » is a mistake French speakers themselves are taught to avoid, and the last option uses future rather than conditional.

questions.stem: In « Je les ai vus hier », why does the participle end in -s?
options: « Voir » is irregular and always adds -s
The direct object comes before the verb, so the participle agrees
questions.explanation: With « avoir » the participle agrees only when the direct object precedes it — which happens when that object is a pronoun. This is the exception to the rule that « avoir » means no agreement.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly combines two pronouns for 'he gives it to me'?
questions.explanation: When two pronouns appear, French fixes their order: me, te, se, nous, vous come before le, la, les. The order is not free and does not follow the English sequence.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I have been learning French for two years'?
options: J'apprends le français depuis deux ans
J'ai appris le français depuis deux ans
J'apprenais le français depuis deux ans
J'apprendrai le français depuis deux ans
questions.explanation: Because the learning is still going on, French keeps the present tense with « depuis ». English switches to a perfect form, and copying that produces the second option, which implies the learning has stopped.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses « y » correctly for 'I am going there'?
questions.explanation: « Y » replaces a place already mentioned and sits before the verb, eliding with « je » to give « j'y ». Adding « là » as well is redundant, since « y » already carries the meaning.

questions.stem: What is the difference between « c'est » and « il est » before a profession?
options: « C'est » is plural and « il est » is singular
« Il est » is past and « c'est » is present
They are interchangeable in every context
« Il est » takes no article; « c'est » takes one
questions.explanation: « Il est professeur » but « c'est un professeur ». The rule is easy to state and easy to forget under time pressure, and getting it wrong is one of the most audible errors an English speaker makes.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I would have liked to come'?
questions.explanation: The past conditional is the conditional of the auxiliary plus a participle. « J'aimerais venir » is present conditional — 'I would like to come' — which is about now rather than a missed opportunity.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of « finir »?
questions.explanation: Regular -ir verbs drop -ir and take -i. The -re group takes -u and the -er group takes -e with an acute accent.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of « vendre »?
questions.explanation: Regular -re verbs take -u: vendu, attendu, entendu, perdu. Each of the three verb families has its own participle ending.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of « faire »?
questions.explanation: « Faire » is irregular and gives « fait ». The common irregulars are worth memorising as a list: eu, ete, fait, pris, mis, vu, lu, dit, ecrit.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of « prendre »?
questions.explanation: « Prendre » gives « pris », and its compounds follow: « appris » and « compris ». None of them look like their infinitive.

questions.stem: Which tense would you use for a description of the weather in a story?
questions.explanation: The imperfect carries background and description; the perfect carries the events that move the story on. « Il faisait froid quand je suis sorti » uses both in one sentence.

questions.stem: Which tense suits 'suddenly the phone rang'?
questions.explanation: A single completed event takes the perfect. Words like « soudain » and « tout a coup » nearly always signal it.

questions.stem: What are the imperfect endings for « je » and « tu »?
questions.explanation: The imperfect runs -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. The first three and the last all sound the same, which makes the spelling the whole test.

questions.stem: How is the imperfect stem formed?
options: From the nous form of the present
questions.explanation: Take « nous parlons », drop -ons, add the endings. « Etre » is the only verb that ignores this rule, using the stem « et- ».

questions.stem: Which verb is irregular in the imperfect?
questions.explanation: « Etre » gives j'etais rather than anything built from « nous sommes ». Every other French verb takes its imperfect stem from the nous form.

questions.stem: How is the future simple stem formed for -er and -ir verbs?
options: The nous form of the present
questions.explanation: « Je parlerai » and « je finirai » keep the whole infinitive and add the endings. An -re verb drops its final e first: « je vendrai ».

questions.stem: What is the future stem of « aller »?
questions.explanation: « Aller » has the irregular stem « ir- », giving « j'irai ». « Etre » gives « ser- », « avoir » gives « aur- » and « faire » gives « fer- ».

questions.stem: What is the future stem of « avoir »?
questions.explanation: « Avoir » gives « j'aurai ». The irregular future stems are shared with the conditional, so learning them once covers two tenses.

questions.stem: Which endings does the conditional use?
options: The future stem with imperfect endings
The imperfect stem with future endings
The past participle with imperfect endings
questions.explanation: « Je voudrais » is the future stem « voudr- » plus the imperfect ending -ais. That is the whole recipe for every conditional in French.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'if it rains, I will stay at home'?
options: Si il pleut, je resterai a la maison
S'il pleut, je resterai a la maison
S'il pleuvra, je resterai a la maison
S'il pleut, je reste a la maison demain
questions.explanation: After « si » meaning 'if', French uses the present even when English uses a future, and « si » elides to « s' » before « il ».

questions.stem: Which tense follows « si » in 'if I had the time, I would read more'?
questions.explanation: The « si » half takes the imperfect and the other half takes the conditional. Two conditionals in one sentence is the error the structure exists to catch.

questions.stem: Where does an indirect object pronoun go?
options: At the end of the clause
questions.explanation: « Je lui parle » — 'I speak to him'. Like direct object pronouns, indirect ones sit in front of the verb.

questions.stem: Which pronoun replaces « a Marie » in « Je parle a Marie »?
questions.explanation: A person introduced by « a » takes « lui » in the singular and « leur » in the plural. « Y » does the same job for a place or a thing.

questions.stem: What does « en » replace?
options: A quantity or a phrase with de
A place you are going to
questions.explanation: « J'en ai trois » — I have three of them. « En » stands in for « de » plus a noun, which is why it turns up with numbers and quantities.

questions.stem: In « Je lui en parle », which order do the pronouns take?
questions.explanation: French fixes the order: me/te/se/nous/vous, then le/la/les, then lui/leur, then y, then en. « En » is always last.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I gave it to her'?
questions.explanation: Both pronouns go in front of the auxiliary, and the direct object comes before « lui ». In the perfect they never split around the participle.

questions.stem: Which relative pronoun is the subject of its clause?
questions.explanation: « Qui » is the subject and « que » is the object. Work it out from the job the word does in its own clause, not from what follows it.

questions.stem: What does « dont » usually translate?
questions.explanation: « Dont » replaces a phrase with « de »: « le livre dont je parle », the book I am talking about. English has no single word for it.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses « que » correctly?
options: Le film dont j'ai vu etait long
Le film ou j'ai vu etait long
Le film que j'ai vu etait long
Le film qui j'ai vu etait long
questions.explanation: The film is the object of « j'ai vu », so it takes « que ». If it were doing the verb it would take « qui ».

questions.stem: Why does « Les lettres que j'ai ecrites » add -es to the participle?
options: All participles agree with the subject
A direct object before avoir triggers agreement
questions.explanation: With « avoir », the participle agrees only when the direct object comes first — here « que » stands for « les lettres », feminine plural.

questions.stem: Which verbs take « etre » in the passe compose?
options: Verbs that begin with a vowel
questions.explanation: The movement group is often taught as a house or as DR MRS VANDERTRAMP; every reflexive verb joins them regardless of meaning.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'she washed herself'?
questions.explanation: Reflexives take « etre », the pronoun stays in front of the auxiliary, and the participle agrees with the feminine subject.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'she washed her hands'?
questions.explanation: The direct object « les mains » comes after the verb, so no agreement is added — the participle stays « lave » even though the subject is feminine.

questions.stem: What does the pluperfect express?
options: An action before another past action
An action repeated in the past
questions.explanation: « J'avais deja mange » — I had already eaten, before the other thing happened. It is the imperfect of the auxiliary plus a participle.

questions.stem: How is the pluperfect formed?
options: Conditional of avoir plus an infinitive
Imperfect of avoir or etre plus a participle
Present of avoir plus a participle
Future of avoir plus a participle
questions.explanation: Put the auxiliary into the imperfect and keep the same participle: « j'ai mange » becomes « j'avais mange ».

questions.stem: Which mood follows « il faut que »?
questions.explanation: « Il faut que je fasse » — expressions of necessity, wish and emotion take the subjunctive. « Il faut » with a plain infinitive avoids it entirely.

questions.stem: What is the subjunctive of « faire » after « que je »?
questions.explanation: « Que je fasse » is irregular, as are « aille », « soit », « ait » and « puisse ». Regular subjunctives are built from the ils form of the present.

questions.stem: How is a regular subjunctive stem formed?
options: From the nous form of the imperfect
From the ils form of the present
questions.explanation: Take « ils parlent », drop -ent, add -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent. Most of those endings look identical to the present.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I want you to come'?
questions.explanation: A wish aimed at someone else takes « que » and the subjunctive. If both halves share a subject, French uses a plain infinitive instead.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'before leaving'?
questions.explanation: « Avant de » takes an infinitive. « Apres » is the awkward one, taking a past infinitive: « apres avoir mange ».

questions.stem: Which structure follows « apres »?
questions.explanation: « Apres avoir mange » or « apres etre parti » — 'after having eaten'. Using a plain infinitive here is the standard error.

questions.stem: What does « en mangeant » mean?
questions.explanation: « En » plus the present participle expresses two things happening at once. The participle ends in -ant and is built from the nous stem.

questions.stem: How do you form the present participle of « finir »?
questions.explanation: Take « nous finissons », drop -ons and add -ant. The -iss- of the -ir group carries straight through.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'the book was written by Hugo'?
options: Le livre etait ecrit par Hugo hier
Le livre a ete ecrit par Hugo
Le livre a ecrit par Hugo
Le livre est ecrivant par Hugo
questions.explanation: The passive is « etre » plus a participle that agrees, and « par » carries the agent. French uses it far less than English does.

questions.stem: What does « on » often replace in everyday French?
questions.explanation: « On y va » rather than « nous y allons ». It takes a third person singular verb even when it clearly means 'we'.

questions.stem: Which sentence avoids the passive the way French usually does?
questions.explanation: Where English reaches for a passive, French often uses « on » with an active verb. All four sentences are grammatical; only one is the idiom.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I would like you to help me'?
questions.explanation: « Vouloir que » takes the subjunctive, and « aider » is regular there, so the « tu » form keeps its -es.

questions.stem: What is the difference between « savoir » and « connaitre »?
options: Savoir is formal and connaitre is the informal equivalent
Savoir is only used in questions and negatives
Connaitre is the past tense of savoir
Savoir is for facts, connaitre for people and places
questions.explanation: « Je sais nager » but « je connais Paris ». English uses 'know' for both, which is why the split has to be learnt deliberately.

questions.stem: Which verb means 'to be able to'?
questions.explanation: « Pouvoir » is can, « vouloir » is want, « devoir » is must and « savoir » is know how to. All four take a plain infinitive after them.

questions.stem: What does « je dois » mean?
questions.explanation: « Devoir » expresses obligation. In the conditional, « je devrais » softens it to 'I ought to'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I have just arrived'?
questions.explanation: « Venir de » plus an infinitive is the recent past. Translating 'just' directly produces something French does not say.

questions.stem: What does « etre en train de » express?
questions.explanation: « Je suis en train de lire » — I am in the middle of reading. French has no continuous tense, so this phrase does that work.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'the more I read, the more I understand'?
options: Plus je lis, le plus je comprends
Le plus je lis, plus je comprends
Plus que je lis, plus je comprends
Plus je lis, plus je comprends
questions.explanation: The paired « plus ... plus » structure takes no article and no « que ». It is one of the fixed frames worth learning whole.

questions.stem: What is the superlative of « bon »?
questions.explanation: « Bon » is irregular: better is « meilleur » and best is « le meilleur ». « Mieux » is the adverb, for doing something well.

questions.stem: What is the difference between « bon » and « bien »?
options: Bon is formal and bien informal
Bon is only used with food
Bien is the plural of bon
Bon describes a noun, bien describes a verb
questions.explanation: « Un bon livre » but « il ecrit bien ». Adjective and adverb, and the same split governs « meilleur » and « mieux ».

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'nobody came'?
questions.explanation: « Personne » can be the subject and still needs its « ne ». « Venir » takes « etre » in the perfect.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I see nothing'?
questions.explanation: « Rien » takes the place of « pas » rather than joining it. Doubling the negative is a mistake in French as it is in formal English.

questions.stem: Where does « rien » go in the passe compose?
options: At the end of the sentence
Between the auxiliary and the participle
questions.explanation: « Je n'ai rien vu » — short negatives sit inside the verb. « Personne » is the exception, going after: « je n'ai vu personne ».

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'neither ... nor'?
options: Je n'aime ni le the ni le cafe
Je n'aime pas ni le the ni le cafe
J'aime ni le the ni le cafe
Je ne ni aime le the ni le cafe
questions.explanation: « Ne ... ni ... ni » keeps one « ne » and drops « pas » entirely. The articles after it stay as they are.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'she made me laugh'?
questions.explanation: « Faire » plus an infinitive means to make someone do something. The pronoun goes before the auxiliary in the perfect.

questions.stem: What does « il s'agit de » mean?
questions.explanation: « Il s'agit de » is an impersonal phrase meaning 'it is a question of' or 'it is about'. It only ever appears with « il ».

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I had already left when she called'?
options: Je suis deja parti quand elle telephonait
J'etais deja parti quand elle telephonait
J'etais deja parti quand elle a telephone
J'ai deja parti quand elle a telephone
questions.explanation: The earlier action takes the pluperfect and the later single event takes the perfect, so the order of the two becomes unambiguous.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'we will have finished by five'?
options: Nous finirons avoir a cinq heures
Nous serons fini a cinq heures
Nous aurons fini a cinq heures
Nous avons fini a cinq heures
questions.explanation: The future perfect is the future of the auxiliary plus a participle. It describes something complete before a future point.

questions.stem: What does « quoique » introduce?
options: A condition, followed by the conditional
A time, followed by the future
A concession, followed by the subjunctive
A reason, followed by the indicative
questions.explanation: « Quoique » and « bien que » both mean 'although' and both take the subjunctive, which is the part that catches people out.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'so that he can understand'?
questions.explanation: « Pour que » takes the subjunctive, and « pouvoir » gives the irregular « puisse ».

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'it is important to listen'?
questions.explanation: With no named subject, an impersonal phrase takes « de » plus an infinitive rather than « que » and a subjunctive.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'the girl I saw'?
questions.explanation: « Que » because she is the object, and the participle agrees because that object comes before the verb.

questions.stem: What is the imperative of « etre » for « tu »?
questions.explanation: « Sois sage » — be good. « Etre », « avoir » and « savoir » all take irregular imperatives borrowed from the subjunctive.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly gives the order 'don't speak'?
questions.explanation: A negative command wraps the verb as usual, and the -er imperative for « tu » drops its -s.

questions.stem: Where does the pronoun go in a positive command?
options: At the end of the sentence
After the verb, joined by a hyphen
questions.explanation: « Donne-le-moi » — in a positive command the pronouns move behind the verb. In a negative command they go back in front.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I wonder whether he is coming'?
options: Je me demande s'il viendra demain hier
Je me demande si il vient
questions.explanation: « Si » elides before « il » but never before « elle ». Here it means 'whether' rather than 'if'.

questions.stem: What does the imperfect add to « je pensais que »?
options: It puts the thought in the future
It reports a thought held over time
It makes the sentence a question
questions.explanation: The imperfect carries a state of mind rather than a single event, which is why thinking, knowing and wanting so often appear in it.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'there were a lot of people'?
options: Il y avait beaucoup des monde
Il y avait beaucoup de monde
Il y a eu beaucoup de monde hier soir
questions.explanation: « Il y a » becomes « il y avait » in the imperfect, and a quantity word takes plain « de ».

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'she asked me to wait'?
questions.explanation: « Demander a quelqu'un de faire » — the person takes « a » and the action takes « de ». The pronoun « m' » already carries the « a ».

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I need to work'?
questions.explanation: « Avoir besoin de » is a fixed phrase, and the « de » stays in front of the infinitive.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'he is interested in music'?
questions.explanation: « S'interesser a » is reflexive and takes « a ». The preposition has to be learnt with the verb, because it rarely matches English.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I am thinking about my exams'?
options: Je me pense a mes examens
questions.explanation: « Penser a » is to think about something. « Penser de » asks for an opinion — « qu'est-ce que tu penses de ce film ? »
